selected.title: Critics warn of 'Santos-sized loopholes' in gas reservation plan
selected.summary: Industry players say draft gas reservation plans are full of carve-outs that will let a venture many blame for rising prices off the hook.
selected.why: Draft gas reservation policy contains contentious loopholes affecting energy market regulation.
selected.fullText: Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news iview listen Loading ABC News News Home Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke Share Share article Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke By energy reporter Daniel Mercer Topic: Oil and Gas Posted Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 5:00am Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 5:00am Mon 12 Oct 2026 at 5:00am Liquefied natural gas ships from Curtis Island in Queensland. ( Supplied: Photopia Studio ) In short: Gas market players say the federal government's draft gas reservation scheme has been weakened by loopholes. They argue that changes to the policy favour the Santos-led GLNG venture, which has been blamed for rising prices on the east coast. What's next? The government is expected to release legislation for the scheme in the coming weeks. abc.net.au/news/critics-decry-santos-gas-reservation-loopholes/107249780 Link copied Share Share article A giant LNG plant blamed by critics for driving up east coast gas prices could largely or totally escape a federal scheme designed to protect local buyers, observers have warned. The Albanese government last month released a draft plan to force gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their production for the domestic market in a bid to force prices lower. But analysts and industry players say the draft is full of loopholes that will allow some exporters to reduce or even eliminate their exposure. They point to the Gladstone LNG project, a plant on Curtis Island in Queensland that is operated by Adelaide-based Santos, as the exporter most likely to benefit. An ABC investigation revealed GLNG had sucked up and exported the equivalent of 20 per cent of eastern Australia's domestic gas demand over the past 10 years. This was because the venture built an LNG plant with a capacity of 7.8 million tonnes a year despite not having nearly enough gas of its own to fill it. By contrast, the other two LNG projects in Queensland — run by global super-major Shell and Australian company Origin along with US firm ConocoPhillips — had overwhelmingly been supplying the local market in net terms. Paul Farrow is unsympathetic to Santos. ( ABC News: Kit Mochan ) Australian Workers' Union (AWU) national secretary Paul Farrow said "Santos-sized loopholes" threatened to turn the government's reservation plans into a joke.
